The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}+c.$ Determine the value of $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
question.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$ 

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-1.$ Therefore, $c=-1.$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13931416/assets/016286e82482af83783f0eef6361591861b564643d4d9f010f2b82999fcaad27.png)

The graph above shows $y=k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c.$ Find the value of $k-c.$
question.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-4.$ Hence, $c=-4.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,-2),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=-2$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}-4 & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{0}-4 & =-2 \\ k-4 & =-2 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
k-c=2-(-4)=6.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=2{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}-4.$

The graph above shows $y=k{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+c.$ Find the value of $k-c.$
question.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=\frac{4}{3},$ hence $c=\frac{4}{3}.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,2),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=2$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+\frac{4}{3} & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{4})}^{0}+\frac{4}{3} & =2 \\ k+\frac{4}{3} & =2 \\ k & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
k-c=\frac{2}{3}-\frac{4}{3}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=\frac{2}{3}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+\frac{4}{3}.$
